title: Iterators & Generators in Python: The Lazy Evaluation Handbook
summary: A dense field guide to Python's iteration model — the iter/next protocol, hand-rolled iterators, generator functions and yield, generator expressions, and lazy pipelines. Covers internals, memory/time trade-offs, itertools, and the gotchas that bite in production.

chapters.title: Iterable vs Iterator: The Core Distinction
points: Definition: an *iterable* is any object that can produce an iterator — it implements `__iter__()`.
Definition: an *iterator* is the object that actually produces values — it implements both `__iter__()` and `__next__()`.
Rule: every iterator is an iterable (its `__iter__` returns `self`), but most iterables are NOT iterators.
`[1,2,3]` is an iterable but not an iterator: `next([1,2,3])` raises `TypeError: 'list' object is not an iterator`.
`it = iter([1,2,3])` returns a `list_iterator`; `next(it)` → 1, 2, 3, then `StopIteration`.
Iterables are reusable (a fresh iterator per `for` loop); iterators are single-use and exhaust permanently.
Container examples: list, tuple, dict, set, str, range, file objects, `collections.deque`.
`range(10)` is a lazy *sequence* (indexable, reusable, has `len`), NOT a generator — a common confusion.
Test at runtime: `isinstance(x, collections.abc.Iterable)` vs `isinstance(x, collections.abc.Iterator)`.
Mental model: iterable = the book, iterator = the bookmark. One book, many bookmarks.

chapters.title: The iter/next Protocol Mechanics
points: `iter(obj)` calls `type(obj).__iter__(obj)` — looked up on the *type*, not the instance (dunder lookup bypasses `__getattr__`).
`next(it)` calls `type(it).__next__(it)`; `next(it, default)` returns `default` instead of raising `StopIteration`.
`StopIteration` is the termination signal — a control-flow exception, not an error condition.
The old protocol fallback: if no `__iter__`, `iter()` builds a sequence iterator from `__getitem__` with integer indices 0,1,2… until `IndexError`.
Desugaring `for x in obj:` → `it = iter(obj)`; loop `x = next(it)`; body; `except StopIteration: break`.
The two-argument form `iter(callable, sentinel)` calls `callable()` repeatedly until it returns `sentinel` — e.g. `iter(lambda: f.read(4096), b'')`.
An exhausted iterator must keep raising `StopIteration` forever — never resurrect (the 'iterator closing' invariant).
Unpacking (`a, b = pair`), `list()`, `sum()`, `in`, `*args` splatting, and comprehensions all drive the same protocol.
Code: `it = iter('ab'); next(it) # 'a'` then `next(it) # 'b'` then `next(it) # StopIteration`.
PEP 234 introduced the protocol in Python 2.2; it is the foundation of every loop construct in the language.

chapters.title: Writing an Iterator Class by Hand
points: Minimal iterator class: `__iter__` returns `self`, `__next__` advances state and raises `StopIteration` when done.
Code: `class Count: def __init__(s,n): s.i, s.n = 0, n` / `def __iter__(s): return s` / `def __next__(s):` guard `if s.i >= s.n: raise StopIteration` then increment and return.
State lives in instance attributes — you manage the cursor manually, which is why hand-written iterators are verbose.
Separate-class pattern: make the container's `__iter__` return a NEW iterator object so the container stays re-iterable.
Anti-pattern: container whose `__iter__` returns `self` — a second `for` loop silently sees an empty sequence.
Inherit from `collections.abc.Iterator` to get `__iter__` for free; you supply only `__next__`.
`collections.abc.Iterable` registration makes `isinstance` checks and structural typing work correctly.
Hand-written iterators still win when you need extra methods, introspectable state, picklability, or a reset.
Comparison: ~12 lines as a class vs ~3 lines as a generator function producing identical behaviour.
Gotcha: forgetting to raise `StopIteration` produces an infinite loop that hangs the interpreter.

chapters.title: Generator Functions and yield
points: A function containing `yield` anywhere in its body becomes a *generator function*; calling it runs NO code and returns a generator object.
The generator object is an iterator: it implements `__iter__` and `__next__` automatically.
`yield` suspends the frame, hands a value to the caller, and preserves all locals and the instruction pointer.
Code: `def gen():` `print('a'); yield 1; print('b'); yield 2` — nothing prints until the first `next()`.
Execution resumes exactly after the `yield` expression on the next `next()` call.
Falling off the end of the function body raises `StopIteration` automatically.
`return value` inside a generator sets `StopIteration.value` — retrievable via `yield from` or by catching the exception.
Multiple yields, yields in loops, and yields inside `try/finally` are all legal and common.
A generator is a resumable function — cooperative multitasking in miniature, not a data structure.
Contrast: a normal `return` destroys the frame; `yield` freezes it on the heap for later resumption.

chapters.title: Inside the Generator Object: State & Frames
points: Attributes: `gi_frame` (the suspended frame or `None`), `gi_code`, `gi_running`, `gi_yieldfrom`.
Four lifecycle states — CREATED, RUNNING, SUSPENDED, CLOSED — inspectable via `inspect.getgeneratorstate(g)`.
The frame object is heap-allocated and kept alive by the generator, which is why locals survive suspension.
CPython flag `CO_GENERATOR` on the code object is what makes the call return a generator instead of executing.
`gi_frame.f_locals` and `gi_frame.f_lasti` let you inspect a paused generator's variables and position.
`g.close()` throws `GeneratorExit` at the suspension point; the generator must not yield again after receiving it.
`try/finally` and `with` blocks inside a generator run their cleanup when `close()` fires or on garbage collection.
Ignoring `GeneratorExit` and yielding anyway raises `RuntimeError: generator ignored GeneratorExit`.
Non-reentrancy: calling `next()` on an already-running generator raises `ValueError: generator already executing`.
Reference cycles involving a suspended frame delay cleanup — do not rely on GC timing to release file handles.

chapters.title: Lazy Evaluation: Compute on Demand
points: Laziness definition: a value is produced only when requested, so work is deferred and possibly never done.
Memory: a generator holds one frame plus the current item — O(1) space regardless of stream length.
Eager `[x*x for x in range(10_000_000)]` allocates ~400 MB; the generator version stays a few hundred bytes.
Short-circuit win: `next(x for x in huge if pred(x))` stops at the first match instead of scanning everything.
Infinite streams become expressible: `def naturals(): n=0; while True: yield n; n+=1`.
Bound an infinite stream with `itertools.islice(naturals(), 10)` or a `break` in the consumer.
Streaming file reads: iterating a file object yields one line at a time — never `f.readlines()` on a multi-GB log.
Pipeline composition: `lines = (l.strip() for l in f)` then `nums = (int(l) for l in lines if l.isdigit())` — each stage pulls one item.
Time-to-first-result drops to near zero; total throughput may be slightly lower due to per-item overhead.
Trade-off: laziness makes evaluation order and side-effect timing harder to reason about and to debug.

chapters.title: Generator Expressions & Comprehension Family
points: Syntax: `(expr for x in iterable if cond)` — parentheses instead of the list comprehension's brackets.
Parens are optional when the genexp is the sole argument: `sum(x*x for x in data)` is valid.
Two arguments require explicit parens: `func((x for x in data), other)` else `SyntaxError`.
A genexp is evaluated lazily EXCEPT the outermost iterable, which is evaluated immediately at creation time.
Consequence: `g = (x for x in mylist)` then `mylist = []` still iterates the original list object.
Late binding gotcha: the filter and expression see the *current* value of closed-over names at consume time.
Comparison row — list comp: eager, O(n) memory, reusable, indexable, has `len`.
Comparison row — genexp: lazy, O(1) memory, one-shot, no indexing, no `len`.
Use a list comp when you iterate twice, need indexing, or the data is small; genexp for a single pass over big data.
`sum`, `any`, `all`, `min`, `max`, `join`, `set`, `dict` all accept genexps directly — no intermediate list needed.
Anti-pattern: `''.join([str(x) for x in it])` — `str.join` materializes anyway, but `sum([...])` wastes real memory.
Python 3 comprehensions have their own scope; the loop variable does not leak (unlike Python 2).

chapters.title: Two-Way Communication: send, throw, close
points: `yield` is an *expression*: `received = yield value` — its value comes from the caller's `send()`.
`g.send(x)` resumes the generator, making the paused `yield` evaluate to `x`, and returns the next yielded value.
Priming requirement: a fresh generator must be advanced with `next(g)` or `g.send(None)` before any other `send`.
Un-primed send raises `TypeError: can't send non-None value to a just-started generator`.
Code — accumulator: `def acc(): total = 0` / `while True: total += yield total`.
`g.throw(ExcType)` raises the exception at the suspension point so the generator can catch and handle it.
`g.close()` raises `GeneratorExit`; the generator should let it propagate after running cleanup.
This turns generators into classic coroutines (PEP 342) — the ancestor of `async def`/`await`.
Distinction: `async def` coroutines use a separate protocol (`__await__`) and are driven by an event loop, not `next()`.
The `@coroutine` priming decorator idiom auto-advances the generator on creation to avoid the priming bug.

chapters.title: Delegation with yield from
points: `yield from iterable` yields every item of the sub-iterable — replacing `for x in sub: yield x`.
It also forwards `send()`, `throw()`, and `close()` transparently to the subgenerator (the real reason it exists, PEP 380).
`result = yield from subgen()` captures the subgenerator's `return` value from `StopIteration.value`.
Recursive traversal: `def flatten(it):` for each item, `yield from flatten(item)` if iterable else `yield item`.
Chaining: `def chain(*its): for it in its: yield from it` — a one-line `itertools.chain`.
Performance: `yield from` avoids one Python-level loop frame per item, so it is measurably faster than manual re-yielding.
Depth cost: each level of delegation adds a frame, so deep recursion still hits the recursion limit.
Gotcha: `yield from` on a string yields individual characters — a classic infinite-recursion bug in `flatten`.
In pre-`asyncio` code, `yield from` was the `await` of its day; today prefer `await` for coroutines.
Guard clause for flatten: `if isinstance(item, Iterable) and not isinstance(item, (str, bytes))`.

chapters.title: The itertools Toolbox
points: Infinite: `count(start, step)`, `cycle(iterable)`, `repeat(obj, times)` — all lazy, all need bounding.
Terminating: `chain`, `chain.from_iterable`, `islice`, `takewhile`, `dropwhile`, `filterfalse`, `compress`, `accumulate`.
`groupby(iterable, key)` groups *consecutive* equal keys — you must sort by the same key first or get fragments.
`groupby` sub-iterators are shared and invalidated when you advance to the next group; materialize with `list()` to keep them.
Combinatoric: `product`, `permutations`, `combinations`, `combinations_with_replacement` — sizes explode factorially.
`tee(iterable, n)` splits one iterator into n; it buffers, so memory grows to the gap between the slowest and fastest consumer.
`zip()` is lazy in Python 3 and stops at the shortest input; `itertools.zip_longest(fillvalue=…)` pads instead.
`zip(*[iter(x)]*n)` is the batching idiom; Python 3.12 adds `itertools.batched(iterable, n)` as the readable version.
`pairwise(it)` (3.10+) yields overlapping consecutive pairs — ideal for deltas and sliding windows.
`accumulate(data, func, initial=…)` is a lazy running fold — running sums, maxima, or any binary operation.
All itertools primitives are C-implemented, so they beat equivalent Python loops on both speed and memory.

chapters.title: Performance, Memory & Complexity Trade-offs
points: Space: list O(n) vs generator O(1) — the single biggest reason to go lazy.
Time: total iteration cost is O(n) either way, but a generator pays a frame resume per item, so tight numeric loops are ~10-30% slower than a list comp.
Latency: generator time-to-first-item is O(1); a list comp is O(n) before the first item is visible.
Genexps beat list comps only past a size threshold; below a few thousand items the list is usually faster and simpler.
Chained genexp pipelines fuse into a single pass — no intermediate collections, no repeated allocation.
`sys.getsizeof` on a generator reports only the object header, not the pending data — misleading but the point.
Random access is O(n) via `islice` and destructive; if you index or slice repeatedly, use a list.
`len()` is unavailable — `sum(1 for _ in g)` costs O(n) and consumes the generator.
Sorting, reversing, and multi-pass algorithms force materialization anyway — laziness buys nothing there.
I/O-bound streaming is where laziness dominates: constant memory over an unbounded network or file stream.
Micro-benchmark honestly with `timeit` on realistic sizes; intuition about generator speed is frequently wrong.

chapters.title: Common Mistakes & Gotchas
points: Single exhaustion: iterating a generator twice silently yields nothing the second time — no error, just empty results.
`list(g)` then `sum(g)` returns 0 — the classic silent-zero bug.
Forgetting the outermost iterable of a genexp is evaluated eagerly, so later mutation of the source surprises you.
Late binding in closures: `(lambda: i for i in range(3))` — all lambdas see the final `i`; bind with a default argument.
PEP 479 (3.7+): a `StopIteration` raised *inside* a generator body becomes `RuntimeError: generator raised StopIteration`.
Consequence: never call bare `next(inner)` inside a generator to terminate it — use `next(inner, sentinel)` or catch it.
Un-primed `send()` raises `TypeError` — always advance once first.
Mutating a container while iterating it raises `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration` (or skips list elements).
Resources opened inside a generator may stay open indefinitely if the consumer abandons it — use `contextlib.closing` or a `with` inside the generator.
`return x` in a generator does NOT yield `x`; it ends the generator and hides the value in `StopIteration.value`.
Debugging: a paused generator has no visible stack in a traceback until resumed, making errors appear at the consumption site.
Truthiness trap: a generator object is always truthy even when it will yield nothing — `if g:` never tests emptiness.

chapters.title: Comparison Matrix: Choosing the Right Tool
points: List comprehension — eager, O(n) memory, reusable, indexable, `len` works. Use for small/medium reused data.
Generator expression — lazy, O(1) memory, one-shot, no index, no `len`. Use for a single pass over large data.
Generator function — lazy, supports complex control flow, `try/finally`, `send`. Use when the logic exceeds one expression.
Iterator class — lazy, stateful, introspectable, can add methods and reset. Use when the iterator is a real domain object.
itertools primitive — lazy, C-speed, composable. Use when a standard combinator already names your operation.
`range` — lazy, reusable, indexable, `len` works, integers only. Use for numeric loop bounds.
Reusability row: only lists, ranges, and containers survive a second `for`; generators and genexps do not.
Decision rule 1: need to iterate more than once, index, or sort → materialize into a list.
Decision rule 2: data is unbounded, huge, or streamed from I/O → generator.
Decision rule 3: one expression → genexp; branching/state/cleanup → generator function; rich object → iterator class.
Decision rule 4: the operation has an itertools name (chain, islice, groupby, accumulate) → use it instead of hand-rolling.

chapters.title: Summary & Field Cheat Sheet
points: Iterable → has `__iter__`; Iterator → has `__iter__` + `__next__`; Generator → an iterator the compiler wrote for you.
`for` is sugar over `iter()` + repeated `next()` + `StopIteration`.
`yield` freezes a frame; `next()` thaws it; `return` closes it and stores the value in `StopIteration.value`.
`send`/`throw`/`close` turn a generator into a two-way coroutine; `yield from` forwards all three to a subgenerator.
Genexp `(…)` = lazy, list comp `[…]` = eager; the outermost iterable is evaluated eagerly in both.
Memory O(1) vs O(n) is the headline win; per-item overhead is the price.
Top three bugs: reusing an exhausted generator, late-binding closures, and PEP 479 `StopIteration` leakage.
Reach for `itertools` before writing a loop — `islice`, `chain`, `groupby`, `accumulate`, `tee`, `batched`.
Build pipelines as stacked genexps for constant-memory ETL over files and network streams.
Debug with `inspect.getgeneratorstate(g)` and `g.gi_frame.f_locals` to see where a paused generator sits.
Rule of thumb: default to lazy for I/O and large data, eager for small data reused more than once.
